look_here_first: Start with flower color. White rosinweed is the standout Silphium in this project because its ray florets are white, while the nearby Silphium comparisons have yellow heads. Then confirm the tough rough/scabrous foliage, often deeply divided, on dry limestone or calcareous prairie.

project_inclusion.range_basis: B129: Travis — UT Plant Resources Center county specimen/index evidence; Burnet — documented Silphium albiflorum occurrence at Doeskin Ranch, Balcones Canyonlands NWR; Mason — TPWD Mason Mountain WMA vascular flora. BONAP/NAPA county mapping used as project distribution cross-check.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Do not mark Hays-local native from the Purola record; that Hays occurrence is explicitly introduced and is excluded from the threshold.

best_field_traits: leaves often deeply pinnately lobed or divided
dry limestone/calcareous prairie and open slopes
morphology_keys.comparison_training: White rays are the fastest split from nearby Silphium. S. laciniatum can also have deeply divided leaves but has yellow heads; S. radula has broad rough sessile leaves and yellow heads; S. integrifolium has broad entire leaves and yellow heads.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Use white rays first, then leaf dissection and texture. Do not treat introduced Hays plantings as native-range evidence.
